idiom_name: plain class inheriting reference equality (AnyRef.equals = eq); case class only for values
implementation_notes: In Scala a plain class inherits AnyRef.equals, which the language specification defines as reference equality (this eq that), and == forwards to equals, so an ordinary class already carries entity identity and eq can be used to ask for it explicitly. The trap is the case class: its instances are compared structurally, by their constructor parameters (the Tour of Scala says compared by structure and not by reference), and the compiler also generates hashCode, copy and unapply, none of which fit a mutable entity - reserve case classes for value objects and events. When identity is a business identifier rather than a reference, override equals to compare the id, keep hashCode consistent and consider opt-in safe equality (Scala 3 multiversal equality via CanEqual, or an Eq typeclass) so comparisons of unrelated types stop compiling.
pitfalls: Declaring the entity as a case class gives structural equality, copy and pattern matching over all fields; a renamed customer then compares unequal and copy silently produces a detached duplicate.
Scala's universal == accepts any type on the right-hand side, so customer == someDto compiles; enable strict equality (CanEqual) or compare ids explicitly where type confusion is possible.
Overriding equals in a non-final class requires the canEqual discipline to keep symmetry with subclasses, and hashCode must follow the same identity, or collections misbehave.
